title: Universal Scaling of the Magnetocaloric Effect in 2D Ising Monolayers and Bilayer
abstract: We report a Monte Carlo study of the magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in two-dimensional ferromagnetic Ising models on square, honeycomb, and triangular lattices with monolayer and bilayer configurations. Using Binder cumulant analysis, we determine the critical temperature ($T_c$) of each structure and find that $T_c$ increases with coordination number, from the honeycomb ($r=3$) to the triangular ($r=6$) lattice. In contrast, the magnetic entropy change ($-ΔS_M$) decreases with coordination number, reaching its maximum for the honeycomb lattice. After normalization by their peak values and appropriate temperature scaling, both $-ΔS_M$ and the field exponent $n$ collapse onto universal master curves for different magnetic fields and across all six lattice structures at a fixed low field. This demonstrates universal MCE scaling independent of coordination number and layer count. Critical scaling analysis further supports the observed universality and power-law behavior. Unlike $-ΔS_M$, the adiabatic temperature change ($ΔT_{ad}$) increases with coordination number, whereas the magnetic Grüneisen parameter ($Γ_M$) follows the same trend as $-ΔS_M$. Although the peak value of $-ΔS_M$ decreases with coordination number, the relative cooling power and cooling capacity remain nearly unchanged due to compensating broadening of the $-ΔS_M$ curves. The field dependence of $-ΔS_M$, relative cooling power, and cooling capacity follows power laws up to $\sim2.6$ T (assuming $J\approx1$ meV). Hysteresis analysis shows that lattices with lower coordination numbers exhibit a faster reduction in loop width with increasing temperature. These results establish the universal scaling behavior of the magnetocaloric effect in two-dimensional monolayer and bilayer magnetic lattices and provide guidelines for designing magnetic refrigerants.
summary: This work uses Monte Carlo simulations on 2D Ising lattices (monolayer and bilayer) to study the Magnetocaloric Effect. The key finding is that after appropriate normalization, the MCE response collapses onto universal master curves regardless of the lattice's coordination number or layer count. This establishes a robust theoretical framework for designing magnetic refrigerants based on fundamental scaling laws.
main_problem: To investigate whether the universal scaling behavior of the Magnetocaloric Effect (MCE) persists across different two-dimensional lattice geometries and layer counts.
main_result: The normalized MCE observables ($\Delta S_M$ and field exponent $n$) collapse onto a universal master curve, demonstrating that MCE scaling is independent of coordination number or layer count in 2D Ising systems.
method: Monte Carlo simulations are used extensively, employing Binder cumulant analysis to precisely determine critical temperatures ($T_c$).
model_or_system: The study uses the ferromagnetic Ising model applied to 2D square, honeycomb, and triangular lattices, considering both monolayer and bilayer configurations.
key_observables: Isothermal magnetic entropy change ($\Delta S_M$), adiabatic temperature change ($\Delta T_{ad}$), relative cooling power (RCP), and cooling capacity ($q$).
important_parameters: Coordination number ($r=3, 4, 6$) and layer count (monolayer/bilayer); magnetic field up to $\sim 2.6$ Tesla.
main_assumptions: The system is modeled by the Ising Hamiltonian; for bilayers, symmetry ($J_{\parallel}= J_{\perp}$) is assumed in some contexts.
figures_summary: Figures schematically show lattice structures (square, honeycomb, triangular) and illustrate the MCE cycle analogy. One figure shows how magnetocaloric properties vary with temperature across different lattice sizes and fields.
paper_structure: The paper details the model formalism, discusses scaling theory and universality, presents results on finite-size analysis of thermodynamic/MCE quantities, covers hysteresis studies, and concludes with implications for magnetic refrigerants.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the concept of universal scaling laws derived from lattice models is fundamental to understanding critical phenomena in many quantum systems, providing a strong theoretical benchmark for comparison.
